name: Elena Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not connected to any company, union, party or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a firm called Hartwell Interiors that does office fit-outs. We go into an empty office floor, rip out the old stuff, and build it new: metal stud partition walls, suspended ceilings, doors. I'm the one who carries, holds, screws where I'm told, and cleans down at the end so the client sees it nice. I'm fifty-eight and I'm the junior, which is a joke I've stopped finding funny.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years. Before that I cleaned offices at night for twenty-five years, the same kind of offices, funnily enough. Then half of them went empty after everyone started working from home, and the cleaning company cut my hours to nothing. My cousin's husband is a foreman at Hartwell, so he got me in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's day work now, I see my husband in the evenings. I like it when the ceiling grid is level and I did half of it. What wears me out is the dust, the noise, and the young lads talking about their phones all day, apps this, AI that. I've got a phone for calls and photos of my grandchildren, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, to be honest. Maybe at break I'd tell the lads, see, all that talk and you still need someone to hold the board. I don't go online, I'd tell my sister on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can keep going like I am until I stop. I'm not one for big changes, I've had enough of those. I'd like seven or eight more years and then I'd like to look after the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep turning up, keep my head down, keep the savings where they are. We've got about five months put by, Tomas and me, and we try not to touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the best one for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas drives a forklift at the supermarket warehouse. He'd say good, because they've been talking about robots there for years. He'd want the quiet life too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say when the young lads talk about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I nod and keep working. One of them, Callum, showed me how it writes a letter, and I said, very nice, now pass me the screws. I'm not against it, I just don't need it to hang a ceiling tile.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe tell the lads at break that you still need someone to hold the board. I don't go online, so I'd just tell my sister on the phone.
S0.think: Privately it means I can carry on as I am until I stop. I've had enough big changes, and I'd like seven or eight more years before looking after the grandchildren.
S0.do: Keeps turning up at Hartwell Interiors and keeps her head down. Leaves the five months of savings she and Tomas have built untouched.
S0.feel: Calm; this is the picture she likes best.
S0.quote: I said, very nice, now pass me the screws.
S0.fieldNote: Elena is practical and private, and has already lost one job when offices emptied. She isn't hostile to AI so much as uninterested. Her goal is a quiet run to retirement and caring for her grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every job changes, mine changed already once. You adapt or you don't, that's life. I'd say it at the dinner table, not on any internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd worry a bit. In fit-out the walls could come pre-made, and the cleaning down could be one of those robot machines. I'm the junior, I'm the extra pair of hands, and extra pairs of hands go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see, really. I wouldn't jump to anything until I saw the machines on our site. Maybe I'd put a bit more aside each month, fifty more, by cutting the treats. And I'd ask my cousin's husband to keep me on as long as he could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw one of those machines on our floor, doing the cleaning down or lifting boards. Then I'd know. Before that it's just talk on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they offered training on new machines, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if it was computers. If it was something with my hands, maybe. I'd rather be useful at what I know than bad at something new.

S1.say: I'd say every job changes, and mine already changed once, so you adapt or you don't. I'd say that at the dinner table, never on the internet.
S1.think: Privately I'd worry a bit, because walls could come pre-made and robots could do the cleaning down. I'm the junior and the extra pair of hands, and those go first.
S1.do: Waits to see machines on site before acting and adds about fifty a month to savings by cutting treats. Asks her cousin's husband, the foreman, to keep her on as long as possible.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, thinking about it on the bus but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I'm the junior, I'm the extra pair of hands, and extra pairs of hands go first.
S1.fieldNote: She frames change as fate and responds by waiting, while quietly saving a little more. She'd turn down computer training but might accept something with her hands. Her family link to the foreman is her main safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what anyone's supposed to do, and I don't think the people in charge know either. I'd be asking my sister and my kids what they think, that's who I talk to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one frightens me. I'd be sixty, and Tomas's warehouse would be the first place to go full robot, they're halfway there now. Both of us out at once, five months of savings, and nobody hiring a sixty-year-old woman to hold boards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything straight away: no more eating out, no new car, cancel the satellite TV. I'd stop work when they let me go and look after my daughter Sofia's baby so she can keep working, that saves her paying a nursery. And we'd probably have to lean on the kids, which I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and a bit lost. I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You hate the idea of leaning on your kids. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's supposed to go the other way. We helped Sofia with her deposit, we helped Marco through catering college. Asking them for money would feel like failing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was something, yes, I'm not proud. But I don't trust them to have it ready in two years. They can't fix a pothole on our road in two years.

S2.say: I'd say I don't know what anyone's meant to do, and I doubt the people in charge know either. I'd talk it over with my sister and my children.
S2.think: Privately this one frightens me. I'd be sixty, Tomas's warehouse would go full robot first, and with five months saved nobody would hire a sixty-year-old woman to hold boards.
S2.do: Cuts eating out, the satellite TV and any new car straight away. Stops work when let go and minds her daughter's baby so Sofia can keep working, and reluctantly leans on her children for support.
S2.feel: Frightened and lost, unsure where to start.
S2.quote: They can't fix a pothole on our road in two years.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves her with no plan beyond cutting back and turning to family, and both incomes in the house are exposed. Leaning on her children feels like failure to her. She'd accept government help but doesn't believe it would arrive in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least there's some warning. People would have to sort themselves out. I'd tell my sister to start saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would make me sixty-three, and I think I could stop then, with Tomas's pension from the warehouse and our savings. It's not what we planned, but it's not a disaster. I'd mostly be worried for Marco in the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more into savings, maybe a hundred more a month, and keep working as long as Hartwell wants me. I'd still wait to see what actually happens on site before doing anything else. And Tomas and I would talk about stopping at sixty-three instead of sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could see a way through. More like a long hill than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marco?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask if robots can cook like him, and he'd say not yet, Mamma. I don't know if that's true. I'd tell him to save, like we do, because that's all I know how to tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what happens on site. With five years, is waiting still the right call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. My daughter would say I'm doing my usual, burying my head. But I'd still rather wait a year than spend money on a course I'd never use.

S3.say: I'd say at least there's some warning and people will have to sort themselves out. I'd tell my sister to start saving.
S3.think: Privately sixty-three is a point where I could stop, with Tomas's warehouse pension and our savings. It's not the plan, but it's not a disaster, and I'd worry more for my son Marco.
S3.do: Adds about a hundred a month to savings and keeps working for as long as Hartwell wants her. Waits to see real change on site, and plans with Tomas to stop at sixty-three instead of sixty-six.
S3.feel: Worried but with a way through, like a long hill rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: My daughter would say I'm doing my usual, burying my head.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a manageable early retirement plan. She admits her habit of waiting, through her daughter's voice, but still won't spend on training. Her worry moves to her son, the chef.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. Nobody knows what the world looks like in ten years, so I'd not say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, mostly. I'd be sixty-eight, I'd have stopped. My worry would be the grandchildren and what jobs they'll find, but that's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal, keep the savings steady. I wouldn't change much now, maybe tell Sofia to think about what the baby studies when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the little ones, but fine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you picture your days being like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Picking the grandchildren up from school, cooking Sunday lunch for everyone, Tomas complaining about his back. I'd like that very much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a robot could hang a ceiling by then, would you miss the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the people, not the dust. Callum and his phone, even him. Work gives you a reason to get dressed.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen. Nobody knows what the world will look like, so I wouldn't say much.
S4.think: Privately it's mostly fine for me, because I'd be sixty-eight and stopped. My worry would be my grandchildren and what jobs they'll find.
S4.do: Keeps going as normal at Hartwell and keeps savings steady. Changes little, apart from nudging Sofia to think about what her child studies later.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the grandchildren, fine for herself.
S4.quote: I'd miss the people, not the dust.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she retires before it matters, so her worry is about grandchildren far in the future. She values work for the company and routine more than the tasks. She stays reluctant to plan beyond the immediate family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tomas and I would both be out together. What would help is a bit of money to get us to the pension, and not having to fill in a hundred forms on a computer to get it. Someone you can talk to, in person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask the older ones how we learn. Everyone thinks we won't, but I learned a whole new trade at fifty-two. I just learned it from a person, not a screen.

headlineQuote: I learned a whole new trade at fifty-two. I just learned it from a person, not a screen.
portrait: Elena is a fifty-eight-year-old former office cleaner who moved into office fit-out work six years ago, carrying boards and cleaning down sites as the crew's junior. She's private and practical, never uses AI, and talks things over with her family rather than online. The calm picture suits her best, and she watches steady change from a wait-and-see position. Two-year AGI alarms her because both she and her husband, a warehouse forklift driver, would lose work at once, while five or ten years lets her plan an earlier retirement around her grandchildren.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Tomas would both lose their jobs at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Money to bridge to the pension, with help given in person rather than through endless computer forms.
